title: Three-dimensional three-photon Stark spectroscopy of a single Rb Rydberg atom in an ultrahigh-vacuum glass cell with eight electrodes
authors: S. A. Spirin, E. A. Yakshina, A. K. Sologub, G. Suliman, A. M. Minnigaliev, V. V. Gromyko, P. I. Betleni, D. B. Tretyakov, V. M. Entin, N. N. Bezuglov, I. I. Beterov, I. I. Ryabtsev
abstract: Quantum computing and quantum simulation with ultracold neutral atoms require Rydberg excitation of individual atoms in atomic arrays. Rydberg states are extremely sensitive to external electric fields, therefore precise three-dimensional control of the electric field is essential. We performed a spectroscopic study of three-photon Rydberg excitation of a single Rb atom in an optical dipole trap in the presence of an external DC electric field. The field was generated by eight electrodes deposited on the inner surfaces of an ultrahigh-vacuum glass cell. The used three-photon scheme of laser excitation of Rydberg \textit{nP} states allows the Stark shift and the splitting of the resonances to be observed simultaneously, which simplifies calibration of the electric field. In addition, in the commonly used two-photon Rydberg excitation schemes, the light shifts can complicate accurate determination of the DC Stark shift, particularly when the external electric field is scanned across different spatial directions, and different Stark components are excited. These shifts are absent in the three-photon excitation scheme used in our experiment. We demonstrated the ability to independently tune the electric field along all three spatial directions and to compensate for stray electric fields. The measured three-photon spectra exhibit Stark shifts and splittings of the three-photon resonance that are in good agreement with theoretical calculations. These results are also of interest for Rydberg electrometry.
summary: The researchers performed three-dimensional three-photon Stark spectroscopy on a single Rb Rydberg atom using a custom UHV cell with eight electrodes. This setup allows precise, independent control over the electric field in all three spatial directions. The results confirm that the measured spectral shifts and splittings match theory, demonstrating a robust tool for quantum simulation requiring accurate knowledge of external field environments.
main_problem: Achieving precise three-dimensional control of the electric field is essential for quantum computing and simulation using ultracold neutral atoms due to the high sensitivity of Rydberg states.
main_result: The experiment successfully demonstrated independent tuning of the electric field along all three spatial directions, with measured Stark shifts and splittings agreeing well with theoretical calculations.
method: Spectroscopic study using three-photon Rydberg excitation of a single Rb atom in an optical dipole trap within a custom UHV cell equipped with eight electrodes to generate controlled DC electric fields.
model_or_system: The physical system is a single Rb Rydberg atom trapped in an optical dipole trap inside an ultrahigh-vacuum glass cell. The field control relies on depositing eight electrodes whose potential solves Laplace's equation, allowing for precise 3D biasing.
key_observables: Stark shift and splitting of the three-photon resonance; ability to independently tune electric fields along x, y, and z directions.
important_parameters: Electric field strengths up to several V/cm; polarizabilities ($\alpha_{P}^{1/2} = 38.8 	ext{ MHz}/(	ext{V/cm})^2$, $\alpha_{P}^{3/2} = 32.5 	ext{ MHz}/(	ext{V/cm})^2$).
main_assumptions: The three-photon excitation scheme is used because it theoretically eliminates light shifts that complicate analysis in two-photon schemes.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the octagonal UHV quartz cell design and electrode placement. Figure 9 compares experimental and theoretical Stark spectra showing field dependence for different magnetic quantum numbers.
paper_structure: The paper details the necessity of 3D electric field control, describes the custom electrode setup and its electrostatic modeling (using MoM), presents the three-photon spectroscopic measurements on Rb atoms, and validates the results by comparing measured shifts/splittings against theory.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controlled experimental platform for probing fundamental atomic interactions in extreme electromagnetic environments, which is crucial for developing reliable quantum simulators based on Rydberg arrays.
